scenes.title: Amazon Q Developer in AWS
scenes.narration: Now we turn from a company knowledge assistant to a developer-focused one. The slide starts with an engineer asking which Lambda functions exist in the AWS account. Amazon Q Developer interprets the question in the context of the AWS console or CLI, then uses permitted account information to formulate an answer. Follow the orange permission box: it is not an omniscient administrator. The assistant can only act within the AWS resources and permissions available to its user and supported integration. The lower three panels show related capabilities. Documentation Q and A explains AWS concepts, CLI suggestions provide relevant command examples, and troubleshooting guidance helps interpret operational failures such as a Lambda timeout. Each is useful in a different moment of a developer's workflow. The warning along the bottom says that proposed actions require review and appropriate permissions. Treat command suggestions as advice to validate before execution, especially when they could change infrastructure.

scenes.title: Q Developer: Infrastructure and Costs
scenes.narration: This slide has two investigation examples. In the upper path, a developer asks why a Lambda function is timing out. Amazon Q Developer examines authorized signals such as CloudWatch Logs, Lambda configuration and X-Ray traces. The evidence column shows a function near its timeout limit, slow downstream response, and time spent waiting on a service. The recommendations column suggests investigating the slow dependency, reviewing retries and concurrency, and adjusting memory or timeout settings only when appropriate. The lower path is a cost question: what drove AWS spend this month? The assistant can analyse authorized cost and usage reports, allocation tags and cost-explorer data to identify a costly workload or region. It then offers cost-optimization recommendations. Notice the caveat along the bottom. Recommendations are not automatic changes; the engineer must verify evidence, calculate trade-offs and approve modifications. Good assistance speeds investigation, but it should not obscure the causal details behind a recommendation.

scenes.title: Amazon Q Developer as a Coding Companion
scenes.narration: This diagram describes an AI-assisted development workflow while keeping the human developer in control. First, a programmer prompts Q Developer with a request such as adding pagination to an orders API. In step two, the assistant proposes code changes and may suggest tests. Step three is deliberately human: the developer reviews the diff, runs the tests, and checks whether the changes are secure and compatible. Only in the fourth step does the developer approve and commit the modifications to the codebase. The lower row shows other development capabilities, including IDE completion, code generation, security scanning and documentation. The orange warning at the bottom is important. Generated code, test results and security findings still require independent review. A model may produce code that compiles but has a logic error, leaks credentials or overlooks an edge case. Use Q Developer to improve productivity, while retaining normal code-review, test and deployment controls.

scenes.title: Amazon Q Developer IDE Extensions
scenes.narration: Here we see Amazon Q Developer inside a real integrated development environment. On the left is Python code using boto3 to list S3 buckets. The example contains hard-coded AWS access-key values. A developer selects the code and asks the assistant to explain or review it. The middle panel shows the answer and an improved snippet using the AWS SDK's default credential provider chain instead of embedded secrets. On the right, a security review flags the hard-coded access key as high risk and recommends using temporary credentials from an approved role. The bottom workflow proceeds through select code, ask Q, review a proposed edit or finding, run tests, and accept only if appropriate. Notice the IDE support callouts at the top, including Visual Studio Code and JetBrains-based environments. The lesson is that AI assistance can identify risky patterns and propose fixes, but the developer remains accountable for reviewing and verifying the actual change before it reaches production.

scenes.title: Q Developer Project Rules
scenes.narration: We finish Module Three with project-specific instructions for Amazon Q Developer. The first panel shows a repository containing a folder for project rules, with a Markdown file describing Python coding conventions. The example rule asks generated functions to include type hints. The second panel shows a developer requesting a function that calculates total price. Q Developer consults the applicable project rule and proposes a typed Python function rather than an untyped example. The third panel shows the developer reviewing and accepting or refining the suggestion. The bottom warning is central: project rules shape model responses, but they are not an enforcement mechanism or a security boundary. Code reviews, linters, tests and policy checks must enforce mandatory requirements. Project-level guidance improves consistency across a team, especially for repetitive conventions. It does not prevent an unsafe or incorrect suggestion from appearing. This closes the agentic AI module by connecting agent reasoning, managed operations, enterprise assistance and responsible development practice.
